    Chapter Overview — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Connection between Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 / Introduction to Jnana Section
    In Chapters six through twelve, Lord Krishna concluded His description of bhakti-yoga. In Chapters thirteen to eighteen, He describes jnana-yoga
    One may ask, “If bhakti is the culmination of the yoga-ladder, why is jnana presented after the section on bhakti?”
    Understanding the connection between the bhakti section and the jnana section will help reveal the reason. In Text 12.7, Lord Krishna promised to save His devotees from the path of birth and death. Chapters Thirteen to Eighteen fulfill this promise by supplying the philosophical knowledge necessary to extricate oneself from material entanglement
    We call this section the “Jnana Section” but in truth the entire Bhagavad-gita is bhakti. The first six chapters discuss how to achieve bhakti through one’s works (karma-yoga). The last six chapters discuss how to achieve bhakti through knowledge. The middle six chapters discuss bhakti itself
    Jnana has its use in assisting our detachment from maya and our subsequent attachment to Krishna. When we utilize knowledge as a means to attain devotion it becomes a part of bhakti
    Without the touch of bhakti both karma and jnana are useless. This is another reason why the discussion of bhakti comes in the middle of Bhagavad-gita, where it can remain in contact with both, karma and jnana, and thus lend them value
    — Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Chapter Quiz · 12 questions
    12 questions · Chapter 13
    1. What is the kṣetra (field) and who is the kṣetrajña (knower of the field) per BG 13.1-2?
    BG 13.2-3 — the body is kṣetra; one who knows it is kṣetrajña; Kṛṣṇa is kṣetrajña in all fields.
    Refs: 13.2, 13.3
    2. How does BG 13.6-7 enumerate the field (kṣetra)?
    BG 13.6-7 details the constituents of the kṣetra.
    Refs: 13.6, 13.7
    3. Which qualities are described as jñāna in BG 13.8-12?
    BG 13.8-12 — 20 qualities such as amānitvam adambhitvam etc. are declared 'knowledge'; what is contrary is ignorance.
    Refs: 13.8, 13.9, 13.10, 13.11, 13.12
    4. What is the Supreme Brahman described as in BG 13.13-18?
    BG 13.13-18 describes the jñeyam — the object of knowledge — paradoxically as having senses yet none, near yet far, etc.
    Refs: 13.13, 13.14, 13.15, 13.16
    5. Per BG 13.20, what is prakṛti the cause of?
    BG 13.20 — prakṛti causes effects, puruṣa is cause of experiencing happiness and distress.
    Refs: 13.20
    6. Why does the soul transmigrate to good or bad births, per BG 13.22?
    BG 13.22 — 'kāraṇaṁ guṇa-saṅgo 'sya sad-asad-yoni-janmasu'.
    Refs: 13.22
    7. What is the upadrasta-anumantā in BG 13.23?
    BG 13.23 — 'upadraṣṭānumantā ca bhartā bhoktā maheśvaraḥ' — Paramātmā is described thus.
    Refs: 13.23
    8. How may one see Paramātmā, per BG 13.25?
    BG 13.25 — 'dhyānenātmani paśyanti kecit ātmānam ātmanā; anye sāṅkhyena yogena karma-yogena cāpare'.
    Refs: 13.25
    9. What is the realisation that liberates per BG 13.28-29?
    BG 13.28-29 — equal vision of the Supersoul and recognition that prakṛti, not the self, performs activities.
    Refs: 13.27, 13.28, 13.29
    10. BG 13.32 compares the supreme soul to what regarding contamination?
    BG 13.32 — 'yathā sarva-gataṁ saukṣmyād ākāśaṁ nopalipyate'.
    Refs: 13.32
    11. What analogy does BG 13.33 give for the sun and the body / field?
    BG 13.33 — 'yathā prakāśayaty ekaḥ kṛtsnaṁ lokam imaṁ raviḥ; kṣetraṁ kṣetrī tathā kṛtsnaṁ prakāśayati bhārata'.
    Refs: 13.33
    12. What is the conclusion of Chapter 13 (BG 13.35)?
    BG 13.35 — 'kṣetra-kṣetrajñayor evam antaraṁ jñāna-cakṣuṣā ... te yānti paramaṁ padaṁ'.
    Refs: 13.35

    Section 1 (13.1–13.7)
    ARJUNA’S SIX QUESTIONS & KRISHNA EXPLAINS THE FIELD OF
    Section overview

    ACTIVITIES AND THE KNOWER OF THE FIELD

    (Text 13.2 – 13.7 answers the 3rd, 4th and 5th questions)

    Krishna explains the field of activities as the body, by which the soul engages within his allotted sphere of activities within the material world
    The soul, the knower of the field, has knowledge of his own field of activities
    Krishna, as the Supersoul, is the knower of all fields of activity of all living entities
    Knowledge is to know the field and its knowers

    Important Words
    • kṣetram — the field
      Neuter accusative. The body is named kṣetra — a cultivated plot — not deha (mere flesh). The word carries the weight of agriculture: something sown, tended, and harvested by karma. Every action plants a seed in this field.
    • kṣetra - jñaḥ — the knower of the field
      Compound of kṣetra + jña (knower). The very form establishes the categorical distinction Kṛṣṇa wants Arjuna to grasp: jña is not the field, jña owns it. The whole chapter unpacks this single word.
    • prakṛtim — nature
      Arjuna's opening question. Prakṛti is the technical Sāṅkhya term for material substance — root of all transformation. The Gītā will redefine it as Kṛṣṇa's energy, not an independent principle.
    • puruṣam — the enjoyer
      The conscious counterpart to prakṛti. Originally Sāṅkhya's silent witness; in the Gītā, the living being who experiences the field's modifications and, ultimately, the Supreme Puruṣa Himself.
    • jñeyam — the object of knowledge
      Gerundive — "that which is to be known." Knowledge in this chapter is not a state of mind; it is a relation to a definite object. The object will turn out to be Brahman, then Kṛṣṇa.
    Arjuna said: O my dear Kṛṣṇa, I wish to know about prakṛti [nature], puruṣa [the enjoyer], and the field and the knower of the field, and of knowledge and the object of knowledge. The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field, and one who knows this body is called the knower of the field.
    Purport

    Arjuna was inquisitive about prakṛti (nature), puruṣa (the enjoyer), kṣetra (the field), kṣetra-jña (its knower), and knowledge and the object of knowledge. When he inquired about all these, Kṛṣṇa said that this body is called the field and that one who knows this body is called the knower of the field. This body is the field of activity for the conditioned soul. The conditioned soul is entrapped in material existence, and he attempts to lord it over material nature. And so, according to his capacity to dominate material nature, he gets a field of activity. That field of activity is the body. And what is the body? The body is made of senses. The conditioned soul wants to enjoy sense gratification, and, according to his capacity to enjoy sense gratification, he is offered a body, or field of activity. Therefore the body is called kṣetra, or the field of activity for the conditioned soul. Now, the person, who should not identify himself with the body, is called kṣetra-jña, the knower of the field. It is not very difficult to understand the difference between the field and its knower, the body and the knower of the body. Any person can consider that from childhood to old age he undergoes so many changes of body and yet is still one person, remaining. Thus there is a difference between the knower of the field of activities and the actual field of activities. A living conditioned soul can thus understand that he is different from the body. It is described in the beginning – dehino ’smin – that the living entity is within the body and that the body is changing from childhood to boyhood and from boyhood to youth and from youth to old age, and the person who owns the body knows that the body is changing. The owner is distinctly kṣetra-jña. Sometimes we think, “I am happy,” “I am a man,” “I am a woman,” “I am a dog,” “I am a cat.” These are the bodily designations of the knower. But the knower is different from the body. Although we may use many articles – our clothes, etc. – we know that we are different from the things used. Similarly, we also understand by a little contemplation that we are different from the body. I or you or anyone else who owns the body is called kṣetra-jña, the knower of the field of activities, and the body is called kṣetra, the field of activities itself. In the first six chapters of Bhagavad-gītā the knower of the body (the living entity) and the position by which he can understand the Supreme Lord are described. In the middle six chapters of the Bhagavad-gītā the Supreme Personality of Godhead and the relationship between the individual soul and the Supersoul in regard to devotional service are described. The superior position of the Supreme Personality of Godhead and the subordinate position of the individual soul are definitely defined in these chapters. The living entities are subordinate under all circumstances, but in their forgetfulness they are suffering. When enlightened by pious activities, they approach the Supreme Lord in different capacities – as the distressed, those in want of money, the inquisitive, and those in search of knowledge. That is also described. Now, starting with the Thirteenth Chapter, how the living entity comes into contact with material nature and how he is delivered by the Supreme Lord through the different methods of fruitive activities, cultivation of knowledge, and the discharge of devotional service are explained. Although the living entity is completely different from the material body, he somehow becomes related. This also is explained.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    Study Notes — Gauranga Priya Dāsa
    Gauranga Priya Dāsa Study
    Bhakti-śāstrī Notes, ISKCON Chowpatty (2009)
    Theme

    Arjuna asks 6 questions about the following subject matters;

    1. ‘Prakrti’ – Material Nature

    2. ‘Purusha’ – The Enjoyer of matter

    3. ‘Kshetra’ – Field in which one can act within the material world

    4. ‘Kshetra-jna’ – Entity which experiences the field of actions

    5. ‘Jnana’ – Knowledge and the process of acquiring knowledge (Explained in Texts 13.3, 13.8 – 13.12 and

    13.24 – 13.25)

    6. ‘Jneyam’ – Object of knowledge

    Swami Sivananda Classical
    Translation
    13.1 Arjuna said I wish to learn about Nature (matter) and the Spirit (soul), the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and that which ought to be known, O Kesava.
    Commentary

    13.1 प्रकृतिम् the Prakriti (matter)? पुरुषम् the Purusha (Spirit or Soul)? च and? एव even? क्षेत्रम् the field? क्षेत्रज्ञम् the knower of the field? एव even? च and? एतत् this? वेदितुम् to know? इच्छामि (I) wish? ज्ञानम् knowledge? ज्ञेयम् what ought to be known? च and? केशव O Kesava.Commentary In some of the books you will not find this verse. If you include this verse also? the number of verses of the Bhagavad Gita will come to 701. Some commentators look upon this verse as an interpolation.We have come to the beginning of the third section of the Gita. Essentially the same knowledge is taught in this section but there are more details.This discourse on Kshetra (matter) is commenced with a view to determine the essential nature of the possessor of the two Prakritis (Natures)? the lower and the higher? described in chapter VII? verses 4 and 5.In the previous discourse a description of the devotee who is dear to the Lord is given from verse 13 to the end. Now the estion arises What sort of knowledge of Truth should he possess The answer is given in this discourse.Nature is composed of the three alities. It transforms itself into the body? senses and the sensual objects to serve the two purposes of the individual soul? viz.? Bhoga (enjoyment) and Apavarga (liberation).The Gita is divided into three sections illustrative of the three words of the Mahavakya or Great Sentence of the Sama Veda -- TatTvamAsi (That thou art). In accordance with this view the first six chapters deal with the path of action or Karma Yoga and the nature of the thou (TvamPada). The next six chapters explain the path of devotion or Bhakti Yoga and the nature of That (TatPada). The last six chapters treat of the path of knowledge or Jnana Yoga and the nature of the middle term art (AsiPada) which establishes the identity of the individual and the Supreme Soul (Jiva Brahma Aikyam).Arjuna now wishes to know in detail the difference between Prakriti and Purusha (Matter and Spirit). He desires to have a discriminative knowledge of the difference between them.

    Swami Gambhīrānanda Classical
    Translation
    13.1 Swami Gambhirananda has not translated this sloka. Many editions of the Bhagavadgita do not contain this sloka, including the commentary by Sankaracharya. If this sloka is included, the total number of slokas in the Bhagavadgita is 701.

    Personal Guidance
    The body is called the field; one who knows the body is called the knower of the field — knowing the difference between field and knower is real knowledge.
    Practical Applications
    • Practice distinguishing between the body (field) and yourself (knower).
    • Use this distinction during physical discomfort.
    • Cultivate witness consciousness as a daily anchor.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I confuse the field with the knower?
    • What does sustained witnessing reveal?
    Analogy

    Imagine a farmer surveying his field at sunrise. The soil, the furrows, the standing crop — all of this is the field. The one who walks its edges, knows what was sown and what has sprouted, is something other than the field itself. The body is that soil; you are the one who walks its edges. Real knowledge begins the moment you stop confusing the two.

    Stories
    Yājñavalkya teaches Maitreyī

    When the sage Yājñavalkya prepared to leave home for the forest, he offered to divide his wealth between his two wives. Maitreyī asked the famous question: "If the whole earth were mine, would it make me immortal?" Yājñavalkya said no — wealth can enrich the field, but it cannot touch the knower.

    He then taught her that the ātman, the knower within, is what is truly to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. The field changes, decays, and is left behind; the knower remains. The Bṛhad-āraṇyaka preserves this exchange as the seed-teaching that the Gītā here unfolds in technical form.
